title: Pacific island nations declare El Niño drought crisis
summary: Fiji and Tonga have declared that severe droughts fueled by the El Niño weather phenomenon are reaching crisis levels in the South Pacific.

Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked reputable news agency proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources A severe drought is taking hold across the tropical islands of Fiji. Fiji and Tonga have declared that severe droughts fueled by the El Niño weather phenomenon are reaching crisis levels in the South Pacific. Drought in the region is strongly linked to the El Niño pattern, which dries up the rains that typically keep tropical islands lush and green. El Niño warms surface temperatures in parts of the Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in wind, heat and rain. The current El Niño is expected to become one of the most powerful on record, experts have warned. The Fiji government said "the ongoing El Niño drought has reached crisis thresholds," forcing the declaration of a nationwide disaster. "Families across Fiji are concerned about the availability of water and the impacts of prolonged dry conditions on their daily lives," Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka said on Wednesday. "Farmers are worried about their crops and livestock. These concerns are real." Under the emergency measures, the Fiji government has the power to ration water , force evacuations and reallocate public funds to disaster assistance. Water sources across much of the country have dropped to worrying levels, local media reported, with scores of trucks dispatched to resupply parched villages. "We cannot control the climate, but we can act early, use our resources responsibly and stand together through its impacts," Rabuka said. Tonga has meanwhile declared a 27-day state of emergency as a prolonged drought causes water shortages across the country. Acting Prime Minister Viliami Latu said the declaration would help emergency services coordinate and deliver drought assistance. "Recent reports have shown the devastating impacts on people, water resources, agriculture and livestock, with potential consequences for the health of people across Tonga," he said, according to local media.
